chunks: He said: Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Muqri reported to me, from Abu al-Qasim Ali ibn Muhammad, from Abu al-Abbas al-Ahwas ibn Ali ibn Mirdas, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Isa al-Rawasi, from Sama'ah ibn Mihran, that Abu Abdillah Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both) said:
Among the signs of certitude is that you will never please the people by earning the wrath of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nor will you blame them for what Allah did not grant you from His favour.

For indeed, sustenance is not driven by the greed of the avaricious, nor is it repelled by the aversion of someone grudging. And even if one of you were to flee from his sustenance as he flees from death, his sustenance would surely reach him just as death reaches him.

key_terms.الرزق: Sustenance (rizq) -- the divinely apportioned provision that every soul receives
key_terms.اليقين: Certitude (yaqin) -- firm, unwavering faith that encompasses trust in God's decree and provision
key_terms.سخط الله: The wrath/displeasure of Allah -- earning God's anger by disobeying Him to please people
key_terms.فضله: His favour/grace (fadl) -- blessings and bounties that God bestows as He wills

ai.seo_question: What does Imam Sadiq say about certitude and sustenance in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) defines the marks of true certitude (yaqin) in three principles: never compromising divine obedience to please people, never blaming others for what God has not given, and trusting that sustenance is entirely in God's hands. This teaching, delivered to his close companions, addresses common anxieties about livelihood and social approval, redirecting focus to reliance on God (tawakkul). The vivid simile comparing sustenance to death -- both inescapable -- was a powerful rhetorical device in early Islamic ethical teaching.
